sections.title: The response toolkit
content: Mitigation: action that reduces the likelihood or impact of a threat
Compensating control: an alternative when the ideal control is impossible
A stopgap, not the permanent fix
examples: Can't patch an old machine yet? Wall it off and watch it closely
say: Knowing the weaknesses and attacks only helps if you can respond to them. Today is the response toolkit: what you actually do to make an attack less likely, or less damaging if it lands.
Pay special attention to compensating controls. When the ideal fix is impossible, you put something else in its place to cover the gap, and you keep working towards the real fix.

checks.question: Why would anyone use a compensating control instead of the proper one?
checks.expect: Because the ideal control is impossible or not possible yet, so an alternative reduces the risk in the meantime.

sections.title: Segmentation versus isolation
content: Segmentation: split the network into zones, PROACTIVE
Limits lateral movement
Isolation: disconnect ONE device, REACTIVE
Quarantine the infected machine NOW
examples: Card payment systems kept in their own zone, away from ordinary office PCs
say: Segmentation is planned in advance. You split the estate into zones so that one compromised machine cannot wander freely to the rest. You are building the walls before anything goes wrong.
Isolation is what you do in the moment. One device is infected, so you cut it off right away to stop the spread, and then you investigate.
sections.analogy: Segmentation is like a hospital split into wards, so an outbreak on one ward stays there, while isolation is moving one infectious patient into a side room straight away. The comparison breaks down because network zones still need controlled paths between them, and those paths are exactly where intruders try to cross.

checks.question: Ransomware has just been spotted on one laptop. Is this a job for segmentation or for isolating the device, and why?
checks.expect: Isolation, because it is the reactive step that cuts that one device off immediately; segmentation is the planned layout.

misconceptions.belief: Segmentation and isolation are just two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Segmentation is a proactive design that divides the network into zones, while isolation is a reactive step that cuts off one specific device.

sections.title: Allow listing and patching
content: Application allow listing: only approved apps run, default DENY
Unknown malware simply cannot execute
Patching: apply vendor fixes for KNOWN vulnerabilities
Useless against zero-days: compensate instead
examples: A finance PC allowed to run only its accounting package and a browser
say: Allow listing flips the usual approach. Instead of trying to spot everything bad, you name the handful of things that are allowed and block the rest. Brand new malware has never been approved, so it never gets to run.

Patching fixes the holes the vendor already knows about. It is essential, but it does nothing for a zero-day, because there is no fix to apply yet. That is exactly when compensating controls earn their keep.

checks.question: Why does allow listing stop malware that no antivirus has ever seen before?
checks.expect: Only approved programs may run, so anything new or unknown is blocked by default.

misconceptions.belief: If every patch is installed, the system is fully protected.
misconceptions.correction: Patches only cover known flaws, so a zero-day can still get through and needs other controls around it.

sections.title: Encryption and monitoring
content: Encryption: stolen data becomes worthless
At rest, in transit, in use
Monitoring: DETECTIVE, watches for indicators
Tools: SIEM, EDR, IDS, NetFlow
examples: A stolen laptop with full-disk encryption gives the thief nothing readable
say: Encryption does not stop the theft. It makes whatever was taken useless. Protect data in three states: sitting on disk, moving across a network, and being processed in memory.

Monitoring is the detective control in this set. It will not block an attack, but it spots the indicators so you can respond. Expect to see security information and event management, endpoint detection and response, intrusion detection, and flow records from routers.

checks.question: Encryption or monitoring: which one is the detective control, and why is detecting still worth having?
checks.expect: Monitoring; it lets you spot and respond to an attack that got past the preventive controls.

misconceptions.belief: Encryption stops data from being stolen.
misconceptions.correction: Encryption does not prevent the theft; it makes the stolen data unreadable without the key.

sections.title: Hardening checklist
content: Change default credentials: removes the easiest attack vector
Disable unused services; close unused ports (Telnet 23)
Remove unnecessary software: fewer vulnerabilities
Host-based firewall and HIPS: device-level blocking
Enforce secure baselines (SELinux, Group Policy) to prevent drift
examples: Telnet on port 23 sends everything, passwords included, in clear text
say: Hardening means stripping a system back to what it genuinely needs. Anything that is not running cannot be exploited, and every program you remove is one less thing to keep patched.

Factory passwords go first, because they are the easiest way in. Then shut the doors you are not using, add a firewall and intrusion prevention on the device itself, and lock the result into a baseline so settings cannot quietly drift back.

checks.question: What does a secure baseline give you that a one-off clean-up does not?
checks.expect: It enforces the hardened settings over time, so systems do not drift back to insecure configurations.

misconceptions.belief: Hardening is done once, when a system is first built.
misconceptions.correction: Settings drift over time, so a baseline enforced by tools such as Group Policy keeps the hardening in place.

sections.title: Matching the fix to the problem
content: Legacy system, can't patch: SEGMENT + MONITOR
Critical web flaw, patch in 2 weeks: WAF as a virtual patch + monitoring
Old server still running unused: DECOMMISSION, wipe data, revoke creds
Junior dev with domain admin: LEAST PRIVILEGE, remove excess rights
examples: A web application firewall blocks the exploit pattern while developers finish the real fix
say: This map is exam gold. When a system cannot be patched, you surround it: put it in its own zone and watch it closely. Those are compensating controls doing their job.
A web application firewall in front of a vulnerable site is often called a virtual patch. It filters out the attack before it reaches the flaw, buying time until the proper fix is ready.

Forgotten servers are a gift to intruders, so retire them properly: wipe the data and revoke any credentials they held. And when someone holds far more rights than their job calls for, trim them back to the minimum.

checks.question: Why is a web application firewall only a stopgap for a flaw in the site's own code?
checks.expect: It filters attacks in front of the flaw, but the flaw is still there; the real fix is patching the code.

sections.title: Pick the mitigation
content: Is it happening now, or are you planning ahead?
Can the real fix be applied right now?
examples: Stolen hard drive, nothing readable: encryption at rest did its job
say: When a question describes a situation and asks for the best mitigation, first decide whether the trouble is live or something you are preparing for. Live trouble usually calls for isolation. A problem you cannot fix properly calls for a compensating control.

checks.question: A company is worried about brand new malware that no scanner recognises. Which mitigation fits best?
checks.expect: Application allow listing, because only approved programs can run.

application.scenario: A small clinic finds ransomware on a reception PC. It also runs an old X-ray workstation that cannot be patched because the vendor has gone out of business, and an intern turns out to have full domain admin rights.
application.question: What would you do about each of the three problems, and in what order?
application.expect: Isolate the infected PC immediately and restore from a clean backup; segment and monitor the unpatchable workstation as compensating controls; remove the intern's excess rights. Isolation first, because that problem is live.

sections.title: Remember the map
content: Segmentation = proactive zones; isolation = reactive quarantine
Patching covers KNOWN flaws only; zero-days need compensating controls
Allow listing = default deny
Monitoring is DETECTIVE
Compensating controls are temporary
say: Two words separate the most confused pair. Segmentation is proactive, decided before trouble. Isolation is reactive, done in the moment.
And whenever a question says the proper fix is impossible, look for the answer that wraps a compensating control around the problem, not one that pretends the problem is solved.

checks.question: Name one mitigation that would make a stolen laptop useless to a thief.
checks.expect: Full-disk encryption, which is encryption at rest.

retrieval.question: If one computer in an office picked up a virus, what would you do first?
retrieval.expect: Disconnect it from the network so it cannot spread, then investigate and clean or rebuild it.

retrieval.question: Why do software updates matter for security?
retrieval.expect: They fix known flaws that attackers could otherwise exploit.

exam_questions.q: Which mitigation reduces attack surface by disabling unnecessary services?
exam_questions.why: Hardening strips a system back to what it needs, removing defaults, unused services and open ports so there is less to attack.

exam_questions.q: Which technique limits an attacker’s ability to move between network segments?
exam_questions.why: Dividing the network into zones with controls between them stops an intruder moving freely from one area to the next.

exam_questions.q: What is the purpose of the principle of least privilege when assigning permissions?
options: Give only the access needed for the job
exam_questions.answer: Give only the access needed for the job
exam_questions.why: Least privilege means each person or process gets only the minimum rights their role requires, which limits the damage if an account is misused.

added_facts: The notes call it 'the core seven' but list six (segmentation, isolation, allow listing, patching, encryption, monitoring); least privilege, from the notes' scenario map, is taught as the seventh. The lesson does not repeat the number seven.

Softened 'TEMPORARY, never a permanent fix' in speech to 'keep working towards the real fix', since compensating controls can stay in place for a long time; the slide still says stopgap and temporary.
Encryption in use explained as data being processed in memory; encryption does not prevent theft, it makes stolen data unreadable without the key.
SIEM, EDR and IDS spoken in full; NetFlow described as flow records from routers.
Telnet sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.
A WAF virtual patch filters the attack before it reaches the flaw but does not remove the flaw.
Isolation first in the clinic scenario because the problem is live.

Same skill tested; teaching never uses the exact phrase 'network segmentation'.

Q3 stem reworded from 'What is the purpose of least privilege?' to 'What is the purpose of the principle of least privilege when assigning permissions?': the original three-keyword stem matched any teaching line that names least privilege, and the term has to be taught. Same answer, same skill tested.
Q1 kept unchanged; rewrote all three explanations.
